entities.name: Patraus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Patraus reigned as king of the ancient kingdom of Paeonia from approximately 335 BCE until his death in 314 BCE, presiding over a period of continued semi-autonomy amidst the expanding Macedonian hegemony. Positioned north of Macedon, Paeonia, under Patraus, navigated a complex geopolitical landscape shaped by the successors of Alexander the Great. His rule is primarily attested through the distinctive silver coinage issued in his name, providing tangible evidence of a functioning royal administration capable of minting currency, a crucial marker of sovereignty in the Hellenistic world.

While the precise circumstances of Patraus' ascension and his familial ties to his predecessor, Lyppeius, remain obscure, his reign occurred within the tumultuous Wars of the Diadochi. Patraus maintained Paeonian independence, at least nominally, despite the overwhelming power of the Macedonian Empire. His silver tetradrachms and drachms, often depicting Apollo or Heracles on the obverse and a horse or horseman on the reverse, served not only as economic instruments but also as powerful symbols of Paeonian identity and royal authority, circulating widely in the region and providing the main historical window into his rule.

Patraus' ability to sustain the Paeonian kingdom as a distinct entity, even as a client state, prevented its immediate absorption into the nascent Hellenistic empires. His reign thus represents a critical bridge period, preserving a degree of Paeonian cultural and political continuity before its eventual complete integration into Macedon. The survival of his coinage suggests a stable, albeit perhaps limited, economy and a recognized royal lineage, influencing regional trade and affirming Paeonian presence on the periphery of the Hellenistic world.

This preserved a separate cultural and political identity before the eventual full Macedonian annexation.
